title: AWS Lambda + SQS: Why Can One Failed Message Cause a Whole Batch Retry?
content:
Suppose AWS Lambda receives a batch of 10 messages from an Amazon SQS Standard queue to process orders:
9 messages are processed successfully. 1 message fails because its data is invalid. You might expect Lambda to retry only the failed message. However, with the default behavior, all 10 messages may be processed again, including the 9 that already succeeded.
1. Why does this happen? When Amazon SQS is connected to AWS Lambda, an Event Source Mapping polls messages from the queue and passes them to Lambda in batches.
By default, Lambda evaluates the outcome of the whole batch:
If the function finishes successfully, the messages in the batch are deleted from SQS. If the function throws an unhandled error, the entire batch is treated as failed. After the Visibility Timeout expires, messages from the failed batch can become available for processing again. A message that repeatedly causes failures is often called a poison-pill message.
The problem is that the failed message is not the only one retried. Successfully processed messages may also run again, causing unnecessary work and increasing the risk of duplicate data.
2. How can we reduce unnecessary retries? AWS supports Partial Batch Responses through ReportBatchItemFailures, allowing a Lambda function to report exactly which messages failed.
Using the same example:
M1–M9: Processed successfully → deleted from the queue. M10: Failed → remains available for retry. Instead of retrying the entire batch, only the reported failed message needs another attempt.
However, ReportBatchItemFailures must be enabled in the Event Source Mapping, and the handler must return the correct list of failed messages. If the handler still throws an unhandled exception, the whole batch can be treated as failed.
3. Is a Partial Batch Response enough? Not completely.
Amazon SQS Standard follows an at-least-once delivery model, so a message can still be delivered more than once.
Alongside Partial Batch Responses, an application should also consider:
Idempotency: Processing the same request again should not cause unintended business effects. Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ): When configured, a separate queue can receive messages that repeatedly fail, so they can be investigated and handled. Key takeaway Partial Batch Responses reduce unnecessary retries, while Idempotency protects data correctness when a message is processed more than once. These approaches complement each other rather than replace each other.

title: Event 1 - FCAJ Buildrathon Kickoff
content:
Event Introduction On September 26, 2026, I followed the FCAJ Buildrathon Kickoff, an event organized as part of the First Cloud AI Journey program at the AWS office in Ho Chi Minh City.
The event covered several main topics:
Introduction to the First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) program. Official kickoff of the Buildrathon. Introduction and networking activities with CMC Global. A presentation by Mr. Truong about a chatbot project designed to support workplace communication. An overview of the Market Slack Bot architecture. Through the presentations, I had the opportunity to learn more about the FCAJ program and understand how an AI application can be developed to solve real-world workplace problems.
1. Introduction to First Cloud AI Journey The event began with an overview of the First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) program.
The presentation introduced the program’s objectives, participation process, and upcoming activities.
This session helped me better understand the learning journey and the project development activities planned for the Buildrathon.
2. Buildrathon Kickoff The next session marked the official launch of the Buildrathon.
The organizers introduced the Buildrathon program and explained how participating teams would work on their projects.
This session gave me a clearer understanding of the Buildrathon’s direction, particularly how participants could apply their technical knowledge to develop solutions for practical problems.
3. Introduction and Networking with CMC Global Another part of the kickoff featured an introduction from CMC Global.
Representatives from the company shared information about their organization and participated in networking activities with members of the program.
The event also included a gift-giving activity, which contributed to a friendly and engaging atmosphere.
Through this session, I learned more about CMC Global and how technology companies can connect with students and technology communities.
4. Mr. Truong’s Presentation on a Chatbot Project One of the sessions I found most interesting was Mr. Truong’s presentation about a chatbot project developed to support communication between different teams.
According to the situation presented, the project involved two teams working in different locations:
Business Analysts (BA): Working overseas. Engineers: Working in Vietnam. Because the teams were geographically separated, exchanging requirements, updating information, and resolving issues could sometimes become challenging.
To address these difficulties, the development team created a Triage Bot to help receive, classify, and process information exchanged between the teams.
What interested me most was that the chatbot was developed to solve a specific workplace problem rather than simply demonstrate AI technology.
5. Triage Bot and Defining AI Responsibilities The Triage Bot was introduced as a tool designed to support information processing and communication between teams.
During the demonstration, I learned how the development team defined the bot’s behavior and operational boundaries through a file called SOUL.md.
Some of the components described in the file included:
Identity: Defines the bot’s identity and role. Expertise: Describes the areas of knowledge the bot should have. Tone & Style: Specifies how the bot communicates and responds. Skills Used: Identifies the skills or tools available to the bot. Domain-specific Protocols: Defines rules for handling tasks within a particular domain. Anti-patterns: Describes behaviors or approaches the bot should avoid. Out of Scope: Specifies tasks that fall outside the bot’s responsibilities. An interesting point was that the bot was not designed to answer every possible request.
Instead, the development team clearly defined its responsibilities, the tasks it could perform, and situations in which it should not respond.
From this session, I learned that building a chatbot involves more than selecting an AI model. Defining its role, scope, operating rules, and response behavior is equally important for ensuring that the system meets user needs.
6. Market Slack Bot Architecture During the presentation, I was introduced to the overall architecture of the Market Slack Bot.
The main processing flow was illustrated as follows:
Slack → Socket Mode → Response Gate → Claude Code
In addition to this main flow, the system included several supporting components:
SOUL.md Memory bot-schedule Internal API Cron and Database Socket Mode Socket Mode uses a WebSocket connection to allow an application to receive events and interact with Slack.
Response Gate The Response Gate is positioned before the bot’s main processing component.
Based on my understanding of the presentation, this component helps determine when the bot should respond instead of processing and replying to every message in the system.
SOUL.md The SOUL.md file defines the bot’s role, communication style, operational rules, and boundaries.
Memory Memory helps retain the context of previous conversations.
This allows the bot to refer to earlier messages within a conversation thread rather than treating every request as completely independent.
Bot Schedule The bot-schedule component supports activities and tasks scheduled to run at specific times.
Internal API The Internal API supports communication and the execution of certain internal application tasks.
Cron and Database Cron and Database support data storage, information management, and scheduled operations.
Through this architecture, I realized that a chatbot used in a real working environment requires multiple components working together. It is not simply a system that sends requests to an AI model and returns the generated responses.
7. Choosing Components When Designing a System One statement from the presentation caught my attention:
“Each piece answered a question I actually faced.”
From my perspective, this means that each component of a system should be introduced to solve a specific problem encountered during development.
In the Market Slack Bot architecture, different components serve different purposes:
Slack: Provides the communication platform where users submit requests. Socket Mode: Establishes the connection with Slack. Response Gate: Controls when the bot should respond. SOUL.md: Defines the bot’s role and operational boundaries. Memory: Maintains conversation context. Internal API: Supports internal task processing. Cron and Database: Handle data storage and scheduled tasks. The main lesson I learned is that developers should not add technologies to a system simply because they are popular.
Instead, they should first understand the problem and then select the components that can solve it effectively.
8. Understanding a Real-World AI Application The Triage Bot demonstration gave me a broader perspective on how an AI application is structured.
Previously, when thinking about chatbots, I mainly focused on the AI model and the API used to send requests.
However, the presentation helped me realize that a practical AI system also requires several supporting elements:
Clearly defined responsibilities and scope. Conversation context management. Memory for retaining information. APIs for connecting different components. Databases for storing data. Scheduling mechanisms for automated tasks. Rules for controlling system responses. These components help an AI application operate more effectively within the actual workflow of its users.
9. Networking and Knowledge Sharing Besides the technical presentations, the kickoff included introduction and networking activities within the First Cloud AI Journey community.
The session featuring CMC Global and the real-world chatbot project provided additional insights into software development environments and how teams with different responsibilities collaborate.
In particular, the example of Business Analysts working overseas and Engineers working in Vietnam highlighted the importance of clear communication during software development.
10. Key Takeaways After following the event, I summarized several important lessons:
Gained a better understanding of the FCAJ program and Buildrathon activities. Learned more about CMC Global and the networking opportunities offered by the program. Gained insights into how different teams collaborate during project development. Understood some of the communication challenges between Business Analysts and Engineers working in different locations. Learned how a Triage Bot can support information processing and classification. Understood the role of SOUL.md in defining chatbot behavior. Recognized the importance of Memory and Context in conversations. Became familiar with the basic architecture of a Slack-integrated bot. Realized that an AI application requires multiple supporting components beyond the AI model itself. 11. Lessons Learned The most memorable part of the kickoff for me was the presentation about the Triage Bot and Market Slack Bot architecture.
Starting from a communication challenge between Business Analysts and Engineers, the development team created a chatbot to support information exchange and task processing.
This example helped me understand that developing an AI application should begin with identifying a real problem, followed by selecting an appropriate model and system architecture.
I also learned that practical AI systems often involve multiple components, including AI Models, Memory, APIs, Databases, Context Management, and mechanisms for controlling responses.
These concepts will be useful as I continue exploring system design and AI application development in the future.

Conclusion The FCAJ Buildrathon Kickoff on September 26, 2026, helped me gain a clearer understanding of the First Cloud AI Journey program and the objectives of the Buildrathon.
Among the topics presented, the session about the Triage Bot and Market Slack Bot architecture left the strongest impression on me.
Through this example, I learned that an AI application requires more than an artificial intelligence model. It also needs supporting components and processing mechanisms designed around real-world requirements.
The knowledge gained from this event provides a useful foundation for further learning about system design and AI application development.

title: Introduction
content:
VPC endpoints VPC endpoints are virtual devices. They are horizontally scaled, redundant, and highly available VPC components. They allow communication between your compute resources and AWS services without imposing availability risks. Compute resources running in VPC can access Amazon S3 using a Gateway endpoint. PrivateLink interface endpoints can be used by compute resources running in VPC or on-premises. Workshop overview In this workshop, you will use two VPCs.
“VPC Cloud” is for cloud resources such as a Gateway endpoint and an EC2 instance to test with. “VPC On-Prem” simulates an on-premises environment such as a factory or corporate datacenter. An EC2 instance running strongSwan VPN software has been deployed in “VPC On-prem” and automatically configured to establish a Site-to-Site VPN tunnel with AWS Transit Gateway. This VPN simulates connectivity from an on-premises location to the AWS cloud. To minimize costs, only one VPN instance is provisioned to support this workshop. When planning VPN connectivity for your production workloads, AWS recommends using multiple VPN devices for high availability.

title: AWS S3: Why Can Storage Charges Continue After Configuring Lifecycle Expiration?
content:
Suppose an Amazon S3 bucket has Versioning enabled, contains 100 objects (each with only one version), and uses a Lifecycle Rule to expire current versions after 7 days.
The developer expects old data to be deleted and storage costs to decrease.
However, after Lifecycle processes all 100 objects, the Object Count can increase from 100 to 200.
The original objects are no longer accessible through their keys in a normal request, but their data still exists and may continue to incur storage charges.
Why does this happen?
1. The reason is S3 Versioning In a versioning-enabled bucket, when Lifecycle Expiration processes a current object version, Amazon S3 does not permanently delete the data.
Instead, S3 creates a Delete Marker as the new current version.
The previous data version becomes a Noncurrent Version.
For the original 100 objects:
100 Current Versions become 100 Noncurrent Versions. S3 creates 100 additional Delete Markers. The total Object Count increases from 100 to 200. The Delete Markers prevent the objects from being returned through normal requests using their keys.
However, the Noncurrent Versions are still stored and may continue to incur storage charges.
Note: Doubling the Object Count does not mean storage costs will also double.
2. An important detail: The Lifecycle timeline Expiration and NoncurrentVersionExpiration do not start counting time from the same point.
Suppose the configuration is:
Expiration = 7 days NoncurrentDays = 30 Example timeline:
Day 0: Upload the object. Around Day 7: The object becomes eligible for expiration. When Lifecycle processes it, S3 creates a Delete Marker and the previous version becomes noncurrent. Around Day 37: If the version became noncurrent on Day 7, it becomes eligible for permanent deletion after another 30 days, assuming no other retention conditions apply. This means the 30-day period starts when the version becomes noncurrent, not when the object was originally uploaded.
These dates are illustrative because AWS uses Lifecycle time-rounding rules and processes actions asynchronously.
3. What should you check if storage usage does not decrease? Instead of looking only at the Total Object Count, check the following:
Increasing Delete Markers: Review Object Versions and S3 Storage Lens metrics such as DeleteMarkerObjectCount and NonCurrentVersionStorageBytes to identify old data that is still retained. Noncurrent Storage not decreasing: Check NoncurrentVersionExpiration, NoncurrentDays, and Lifecycle Rule filters. If NewerNoncurrentVersions is configured, both the age and version-count conditions must be satisfied. Incomplete Multipart Uploads: Check IncompleteMultipartUploadStorageBytes and consider using AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload to clean up unfinished uploads. Storage costs not decreasing as expected: Review Storage Classes, minimum storage duration charges, and AWS Billing information. Also, if Noncurrent Versions have been permanently deleted but Delete Markers remain, review the Expired Object Delete Marker cleanup mechanism.
Another important detail is that Lifecycle actions are asynchronous. However, AWS applies the relevant billing changes when objects become eligible for expiration, even if physical deletion happens later. Noncurrent Versions that have not yet become eligible for expiration may still incur storage charges.
4. A practical example Suppose a restaurant recommendation website uses Amazon S3 to store user-uploaded images.
When a user clicks “Delete Image”, the application may remove the image metadata or create a Delete Marker, while older image versions remain in S3.
Therefore, designing a data deletion feature requires considering:
Data recovery requirements. Storage costs. Permanent deletion requirements. Key takeaway Lifecycle Expiration does not necessarily mean Permanent Deletion in a versioning-enabled S3 bucket.
Do not check only whether an object has disappeared. Also review the stored object versions and make sure the Lifecycle configuration matches your data retention requirements.

title: Event 2 - AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi
content:
Event Introduction On September 29, 2026, I attended a viewing party in Ho Chi Minh City to follow AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi, an event held in Hanoi, Vietnam.
The event focused on cloud computing, artificial intelligence, software development, and modern technology solutions used by businesses.
Through the presentations, I had the opportunity to learn more about cloud architecture, AI Agents, AI-assisted software development, cloud security, and system operations.
Event Information Event Name: AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi. Date: September 29, 2026. Main Event Location: Hanoi, Vietnam. My Attendance Location: Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. Participation Format: Viewing party, following the event presentations. Topics Explored 1. Cloud Architecture and System Scalability One of the topics discussed during the event was how to design systems that can serve large numbers of users while maintaining performance and availability.
The presentations introduced several challenges in distributed systems, especially when the amount of data and the number of requests increase.
I also learned about Amazon Dynamo, a key-value storage system designed to support scalability and availability in distributed environments.
This session helped me understand that cloud application development involves more than implementing features. Developers must also consider scalability, reliability, and operational efficiency.
2. AI Agents and Modern AI Applications Another topic I found interesting was the development of AI Agents and AI-native applications.
The presentations explored how AI Agents can support workflow automation, task processing, and improved productivity in organizations.
However, deploying AI in real-world environments also presents several challenges:
Controlling the quality of AI-generated outputs. Ensuring that AI systems operate within their intended scope. Reviewing and validating AI-generated results. Maintaining human oversight for important tasks. From this session, I realized that building an AI application involves more than connecting to a language model. A reliable system also requires a well-designed workflow, testing, and appropriate management mechanisms.
3. AI-Assisted Software Development The event also introduced new approaches to software development, particularly the use of AI Coding Assistants and AI Agents to support developers.
AI tools can assist programmers in understanding source code, suggesting solutions, and handling certain development tasks.
However, AI-assisted development still needs to be combined with essential software engineering practices, including:
Requirements analysis. System architecture design. Functional testing. Security assessment. Monitoring and continuous improvement. This session helped me recognize that AI tools can improve development productivity, but programming knowledge and problem-solving skills remain essential.
4. Cloud Security and System Operations Security is an important consideration when developing and deploying cloud applications.
The presentations covered topics such as vulnerability detection, automated security testing, and approaches to maintaining secure system operations.
I learned that security should not be considered only after an application has been completed. Instead, it should be integrated throughout the development lifecycle.
In addition, system monitoring plays an important role in identifying issues and supporting incident response.
5. AWS Solutions and AI Adoption in Enterprises Another topic discussed during the event was how businesses can combine AWS services with artificial intelligence to develop technology solutions.
The presentations highlighted the role of cloud platforms in providing infrastructure, supporting data processing, deploying AI applications, and monitoring system operations.
Through this topic, I gained a broader understanding of how Cloud and AI technologies can work together to address practical business challenges.
Key Takeaways After following the presentations, I summarized several important lessons:
Gained a better understanding of scalability and availability in cloud systems. Learned more about distributed systems and the challenges of supporting large numbers of users. Explored the development of AI Agents and AI-native applications. Recognized the role of AI in supporting software development and workflow automation. Understood that AI-generated results still require evaluation and validation. Learned more about cloud security, monitoring, and system operations. Gained insights into how AWS can support businesses in developing and deploying AI solutions. Connection to My Personal Project I am currently developing a restaurant recommendation and itinerary planning application for Ho Chi Minh City.
Based on the topics presented at the event, I identified several concepts that may be useful for my project.
First, developing a recommendation system requires attention to data quality and the ability to process user requests effectively. As the number of restaurants and users increases, system scalability may also become an important consideration.
In addition, the AI-related topics helped me recognize the importance of evaluating recommendation results rather than relying entirely on system-generated outputs.
The discussions about cloud security and operations also provided a foundation for exploring AWS deployment options in the future.
These are potential areas for future development. They do not mean that all the technologies discussed at the event have already been implemented in my project.
Personal Experience Attending the viewing party gave me an opportunity to explore Cloud Computing and AI through presentations about real-world applications.
Among the topics discussed, I was particularly interested in AI Agents and how AI can support the software development process.
Some concepts related to distributed systems and cloud architecture were still relatively new to me, so I plan to continue learning through documentation and practical exercises.
Overall, the event broadened my perspective on AI and Cloud technologies and helped me recognize the importance of combining programming, system design, and application operations.

title: Proposal
content:
⚠️ Note: The information below is for reference purposes only. Please do not copy verbatim for your report, including this warning.
In this section, you need to summarize the contents of the workshop that you plan to conduct.
IoT Weather Platform for Lab Research A Unified AWS Serverless Solution for Real-Time Weather Monitoring 1. Executive Summary The IoT Weather Platform is designed for the ITea Lab team in Ho Chi Minh City to enhance weather data collection and analysis. It supports up to 5 weather stations, with potential scalability to 10-15, utilizing Raspberry Pi edge devices with ESP32 sensors to transmit data via MQTT. The platform leverages AWS Serverless services to deliver real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, and cost efficiency, with access restricted to 5 lab members via Amazon Cognito.
2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? Current weather stations require manual data collection, becoming unmanageable with multiple units. There is no centralized system for real-time data or analytics, and third-party platforms are costly and overly complex.
The Solution The platform uses AWS IoT Core to ingest MQTT data, AWS Lambda and API Gateway for processing, Amazon S3 for storage (including a data lake), and AWS Glue Crawlers and ETL jobs to extract, transform, and load data from the S3 data lake to another S3 bucket for analysis. AWS Amplify with Next.js provides the web interface, and Amazon Cognito ensures secure access. Similar to Thingsboard and CoreIoT, users can register new devices and manage connections, though this platform operates on a smaller scale and is designed for private use. Key features include real-time dashboards, trend analysis, and low operational costs.
Benefits and Return on Investment The solution establishes a foundational resource for lab members to develop a larger IoT platform, serving as a study resource, and provides a data foundation for AI enthusiasts for model training or analysis. It reduces manual reporting for each station via a centralized platform, simplifying management and maintenance, and improves data reliability. Monthly costs are $0.66 USD per the AWS Pricing Calculator, with a 12-month total of $7.92 USD. All IoT equipment costs are covered by the existing weather station setup, eliminating additional development expenses. The break-even period of 6-12 months is achieved through significant time savings from reduced manual work.
3. Solution Architecture The platform employs a serverless AWS architecture to manage data from 5 Raspberry Pi-based stations, scalable to 15. Data is ingested via AWS IoT Core, stored in an S3 data lake, and processed by AWS Glue Crawlers and ETL jobs to transform and load it into another S3 bucket for analysis. Lambda and API Gateway handle additional processing, while Amplify with Next.js hosts the dashboard, secured by Cognito. The architecture is detailed below:
AWS Services Used AWS IoT Core: Ingests MQTT data from 5 stations, scalable to 15. AWS Lambda: Processes data and triggers Glue jobs (two functions). Amazon API Gateway: Facilitates web app communication. Amazon S3: Stores raw data in a data lake and processed outputs (two buckets). AWS Glue: Crawlers catalog data, and ETL jobs transform and load it. AWS Amplify: Hosts the Next.js web interface. Amazon Cognito: Secures access for lab users. Component Design Edge Devices: Raspberry Pi collects and filters sensor data, sending it to IoT Core. Data Ingestion: AWS IoT Core receives MQTT messages from the edge devices. Data Storage: Raw data is stored in an S3 data lake; processed data is stored in another S3 bucket. Data Processing: AWS Glue Crawlers catalog the data, and ETL jobs transform it for analysis. Web Interface: AWS Amplify hosts a Next.js app for real-time dashboards and analytics. User Management: Amazon Cognito manages user access, allowing up to 5 active accounts. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases This project has two parts—setting up weather edge stations and building the weather platform—each following 4 phases:
Build Theory and Draw Architecture: Research Raspberry Pi setup with ESP32 sensors and design the AWS serverless architecture (1 month pre-internship) Calculate Price and Check Practicality: Use AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate costs and adjust if needed (Month 1). Fix Architecture for Cost or Solution Fit: Tweak the design (e.g., optimize Lambda with Next.js) to stay cost-effective and usable (Month 2). Develop, Test, and Deploy: Code the Raspberry Pi setup, AWS services with CDK/SDK, and Next.js app, then test and release to production (Months 2-3). Technical Requirements
Weather Edge Station: Sensors (temperature, humidity, rainfall, wind speed), a microcontroller (ESP32), and a Raspberry Pi as the edge device. Raspberry Pi runs Raspbian, handles Docker for filtering, and sends 1 MB/day per station via MQTT over Wi-Fi. Weather Platform: Practical knowledge of AWS Amplify (hosting Next.js), Lambda (minimal use due to Next.js), AWS Glue (ETL), S3 (two buckets), IoT Core (gateway and rules), and Cognito (5 users). Use AWS CDK/SDK to code interactions (e.g., IoT Core rules to S3). Next.js reduces Lambda workload for the fullstack web app. 5. Timeline & Milestones Project Timeline
Pre-Internship (Month 0): 1 month for planning and old station review. Internship (Months 1-3): 3 months. Month 1: Study AWS and upgrade hardware. Month 2: Design and adjust architecture. Month 3: Implement, test, and launch. Post-Launch: Up to 1 year for research. 6. Budget Estimation You can find the budget estimation on the AWS Pricing Calculator.
Or you can download the Budget Estimation File.
Infrastructure Costs AWS Services: AWS Lambda: $0.00/month (1,000 requests, 512 MB storage). S3 Standard: $0.15/month (6 GB, 2,100 requests, 1 GB scanned). Data Transfer: $0.02/month (1 GB inbound, 1 GB outbound). AWS Amplify: $0.35/month (256 MB, 500 ms requests). Amazon API Gateway: $0.01/month (2,000 requests). AWS Glue ETL Jobs: $0.02/month (2 DPUs). AWS Glue Crawlers: $0.07/month (1 crawler). MQTT (IoT Core): $0.08/month (5 devices, 45,000 messages). Total: $0.7/month, $8.40/12 months
Hardware: $265 one-time (Raspberry Pi 5 and sensors). 7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix Network Outages: Medium impact, medium probability. Sensor Failures: High impact, low probability. Cost Overruns: Medium impact, low probability. Mitigation Strategies Network: Local storage on Raspberry Pi with Docker. Sensors: Regular checks and spares. Cost: AWS budget alerts and optimization. Contingency Plans Revert to manual methods if AWS fails. Use CloudFormation for cost-related rollbacks. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements: Real-time data and analytics replace manual processes.
Scalable to 10-15 stations.
Long-term Value 1-year data foundation for AI research.
Reusable for future projects.

title: Published Blog Posts
content:
Throughout my journey of learning and exploring Amazon Web Services (AWS), I have written and shared technical articles analyzing real-world scenarios that developers and cloud engineers may encounter when building, operating, and securing cloud-based systems.
Below are three blog posts I have published, focusing on how AWS services work, commonly overlooked issues, and practical solutions.
Blog 1 - AWS LAMBDA + SQS: WHY CAN ONE FAILED MESSAGE CAUSE AN ENTIRE BATCH TO BE PROCESSED AGAIN? This article explores batch message processing when integrating AWS Lambda with Amazon SQS. By default, if a single message fails during processing, the entire batch may become available for reprocessing, potentially resulting in duplicate processing of messages that have already succeeded.
The article also introduces Partial Batch Response, Idempotency, and important practices for building more reliable message-processing systems.
Read the original post on Facebook
Blog 2 - AMAZON S3: WHY CAN STORAGE COSTS CONTINUE EVEN AFTER DELETING FILES? This article examines how S3 Versioning and Lifecycle Rules interact. When Versioning is enabled, deleting an object may only create a Delete Marker, while previous object versions remain stored and continue to incur storage costs.
It explains the roles of Delete Markers and Noncurrent Versions, as well as how to configure Lifecycle rules appropriately to manage data and optimize Amazon S3 storage costs.
Read the original post on Facebook
Blog 3 - AWS API GATEWAY: HOW CAN CACHING AN ALLOW RESPONSE UNINTENTIONALLY GRANT ACCESS TO ANOTHER ROUTE? This article analyzes an authorization risk involving Amazon API Gateway HTTP API, Lambda Authorizers, Simple Responses, and Authorizer Caching.
If the cache key is based only on user identity without distinguishing between routes, an Allow result from one route may be reused for another route, potentially granting unintended access.
The article explains the underlying caching mechanism and possible mitigations, such as including $context.routeKey in the Identity Sources or designing appropriate route-specific authorization policies.

title: AWS API Gateway: How Can Incorrect Authorizer Caching Allow Regular Users to Access Admin APIs?
content:
When an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API uses a Lambda Authorizer with Simple Responses and Authorizer Caching, a cache key based only on the Authorization token may allow an authorization result from one route to be reused for another.
This can result in unintended access to protected API routes.
Suppose an application uses Amazon API Gateway HTTP API with a Lambda Authorizer to control access.
The system has two routes:
GET /restaurants: Accessible to regular users. GET /admin/restaurants: Accessible only to administrators. Both routes share the same Lambda Authorizer, with Simple Responses and Authorizer Caching enabled.
The developer expects regular users to access /restaurants but be denied access to /admin/restaurants.
However, if caching is configured incorrectly, an Allow result from the first route may be reused for the second route without checking permissions again.
1. Why does this happen? When Authorizer Caching is enabled, API Gateway uses Identity Sources to generate a cache key.
This key determines when a previously stored authorization result can be reused.
For example, suppose the only Identity Source is:
$request.header.Authorization Two requests using the same Authorization header will have the same cache key, even if they access different routes that share the authorizer.
Step 1: A regular user accesses a public API route A regular user sends:
GET /restaurants The Lambda Authorizer checks the token and route permissions.
Since the user is allowed to access this route, it returns:
{ "isAuthorized": true } API Gateway caches this result using the Authorization token.
Step 2: The user accesses an Admin API route While the cache TTL is still valid, the same user sends:
GET /admin/restaurants If the Lambda Authorizer were invoked again, it should return:
{ "isAuthorized": false } The user does not have administrator permissions.
However, because the second request uses the same Authorization token, API Gateway may find the previously cached true result.
Instead of invoking the Lambda Authorizer again, API Gateway reuses the cached Allow decision.
As a result, the request may pass API Gateway authorization even though the user does not have permission to access the Admin route.
Root cause: The cache key does not distinguish between routes, while a Simple Response returns a Boolean Allow/Deny decision without defining permissions for individual API resources.
This is an authorization configuration risk, not a default security vulnerability in AWS.
2. How can this be prevented? Solution 1 — Include the Route Key in the Cache Key Instead of using only the Authorization token, configure the Identity Sources as:
$request.header.Authorization $context.routeKey API Gateway will then generate a cache key based on both the token and the route key.
For example:
Token A + GET /restaurants → Allow Token A + GET /admin/restaurants → Deny This allows authorization results to be cached separately for each route, preventing an Allow result from one route from being incorrectly reused for another.
Important: $context.routeKey distinguishes API routes, but it does not distinguish individual resources within the same route.
For example:
GET /orders/100 GET /orders/200 Both requests may match the same route:
GET /orders/{id} If authorization depends on the ownership of each order, adding $context.routeKey alone is not enough.
Solution 2 — Use an IAM Policy Response Instead of returning only a Boolean Allow/Deny result, a Lambda Authorizer can return an IAM Policy.
This allows the authorizer to define permissions for specific API resources and HTTP methods.
An IAM Policy provides more granular access control than a Simple Response.
However, using an IAM Policy does not automatically solve every caching problem.
The policy’s resource scope and cache configuration must still match the application’s authorization requirements.
Solution 3 — Enforce Authorization in the Backend API Gateway authorization should not always be the only security layer protecting application data.
For example, even if a user is allowed to call:
GET /orders/{id} That does not mean they should be able to access every order.
The backend must still verify whether the requested order belongs to the user or is otherwise accessible to them.
This is especially important for applications that require authorization at the individual resource level.
3. Practical lessons When enabling Lambda Authorizer Caching, three factors deserve particular attention:
Cache Key: Do the Identity Sources include the information that affects authorization decisions? Authorization Response: Is a Boolean Allow/Deny response suitable when different routes require different permissions? Cache TTL: If a user’s permissions change, how long can a cached authorization result remain valid? During testing, Authorizer Caching can be temporarily disabled by setting:
authorizerResultTtlInSeconds = 0 This allows authorization behavior to be observed when the authorizer is invoked again for each request.
Note: This example focuses specifically on Lambda Authorizers for HTTP APIs with caching enabled, especially when using Simple Responses. It should not be confused with JWT Authorizer behavior.
Conclusion Authorizer Caching reduces Lambda Authorizer invocations, which can improve performance and reduce request latency.
However, when the cache key does not reflect the required authorization scope, an Allow result may be reused beyond its intended context.
The key lesson is not simply to add $context.routeKey, but to design cache keys around the information that determines access permissions.
A configuration that improves application performance can also introduce security risks if it is not designed and tested carefully.

title: Event 3 - FCAJ Mini Meeting
content:
Event Introduction On October 24, 2026, I attended the FCAJ Mini Meeting, a technical knowledge-sharing event organized within the First Cloud AI Journey community.
The meeting covered several topics related to artificial intelligence and cloud computing, including Vietnamese Voice AI, AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM), AWS Security Agent, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
Through the presentations, I had an opportunity to learn more about how these technologies can be used in real-world systems. This report summarizes my understanding based on my notes and the presentation materials from the event.
Event Information Event Name: FCAJ Mini Meeting. Date: October 24, 2026. Role: Attendee. Main Topics: Voice AI, AWS RAM, AWS Security Agent, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. 1. Hear, Think, Speak — Building Vietnamese Voice AI Kiet Tran, an AI Engineer at Revve AI, presented Hear, Think, Speak: Building a Vietnamese Voice-AI Contact Center on AWS.
The session introduced how voice-based AI systems can be developed for applications such as customer service contact centers and interviews.
One point I found interesting was that a Voice AI system needs more than accurate answers. It must also detect when a user has finished speaking, process the request, and respond with sufficiently low latency to maintain a natural conversation.
Three Approaches to Building Voice Agents The presentation introduced three approaches:
Cascade: Divides processing into ASR → LLM → TTS. Speech is converted into text, processed by a language model, and then transformed into a spoken response. Speech-to-Speech (S2S): Uses a speech model to process audio inputs and generate audio outputs. Full Duplex S2S: Aims to support simultaneous listening and speaking, creating a more natural conversational experience. According to the presentation, the development team continued using Cascade in production while experimenting with Speech-to-Speech approaches.
For their Vietnamese-language use case, Cascade offered flexibility in selecting individual components and controlling responses through an intermediate text-processing stage.
This session helped me understand that Voice AI architecture should be selected according to practical requirements, including speech quality, response latency, logging, and the ability to improve individual components.
Call Processing and AWS Architecture The architecture slides introduced several components working together:
SIP Server and Media Server. Noise Cancellation. Turn Detection. Speech-to-Text. LLM with a Flow Engine. Text-to-Speech. The presentation also described Revve’s deployment architecture within a single AWS Region and the customer’s AWS account.
In addition, the speaker shared a proof of concept for a Vietnamese bank. The workflow involved receiving requests, verifying information, identifying user intent, and handling requests through APIs or transferring them to human agents.
This example helped me realize that a real-world Voice AI application requires both AI technologies and well-designed business workflows.
2. AWS Resource Access Manager — Cross-Account Resource Sharing Long Huynh presented AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM).
The session began by discussing the challenges organizations face when managing multiple AWS accounts and sharing resources between them.
The main topics included:
Multi-account Challenge: Difficulties in organizing and managing resources across multiple AWS accounts. AWS RAM: An introduction to the service and its resource-sharing capabilities. Resource Share: Defining shared resources, recipients, and permissions. Sharing Workflow: Understanding the process of sharing resources between AWS accounts. Regions and Availability Zone IDs: Important considerations regarding resource scope and deployment locations. RAM in a Landing Zone: How resource sharing can support enterprise AWS environments. According to my notes, the speaker also mentioned that AWS RAM supports resource sharing across more than 40 AWS services.
My main takeaway was that organizations need to clearly identify which resources are shared, which accounts can access them, and what permissions are granted.
This session gave me an initial understanding of managing AWS infrastructure across multiple accounts rather than working with individual services in a single account.
3. AWS Security Agent — Securing Web Applications Thinh presented Securing Your Web Apps With AWS Security Agent.
The session introduced an AI Agent-assisted approach to reviewing web application security.
One topic that caught my attention was Design Security Review.
According to the presentation, the tool can use several types of input, including:
System design documents written in Markdown. Terraform infrastructure configuration files. Configured security requirement packs. These inputs can support the process of evaluating a system design against defined security requirements.
This helped me understand that security reviews do not necessarily need to wait until an application is fully developed. Potential security risks can also be considered during the design stage.
The speaker also discussed costs in a section titled The Pricing Reality.
From this topic, I learned that organizations should consider the assessment scope and the amount of time an AI Agent spends performing tasks when estimating usage costs.
4. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore — Runtime and Memory Xuan An presented Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, focusing on Runtime and Memory Architecture.
The session began with an introduction to AI Agents, Agentic AI, and Agentic Systems before exploring several AgentCore components.
AgentCore Runtime The Runtime section gave me an overview of an execution environment designed for AI Agent applications.
It helped me understand that an AI Agent system needs mechanisms for executing and managing tasks rather than simply sending a request to an AI model and returning a response.
AgentCore Memory The Memory section introduced how interaction information can be organized into events and related data fields.
Some concepts discussed included:
Memory ID: Identifies a memory resource. Actor ID: Identifies an actor involved in an interaction. Session ID: Identifies an interaction session. Payload: Contains the recorded interaction data. Timestamp: Records when an event occurred. Branch: Represents information associated with an interaction branch. The presentation helped me visualize how information from interaction sessions can be structured and managed to support AI Agent applications.
The meeting also briefly mentioned Kiro Crew and App & Extensibility. These are topics I would like to explore further.
5. Key Takeaways After attending the FCAJ Mini Meeting, I summarized several important lessons:
Understood the basic differences between Cascade, Speech-to-Speech, and Full Duplex Speech-to-Speech. Learned how Voice AI systems combine audio processing, AI models, APIs, and business workflows. Gained an introduction to AWS RAM and resource sharing across multiple AWS accounts. Recognized the value of reviewing application security during the system design stage. Became more aware of potential costs when using AI-assisted security assessment tools. Learned about Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime and Memory. Gained an initial understanding of how interaction data and context can be organized within AI Agent systems. 6. Connection to My Personal Project I am currently developing a restaurant recommendation and itinerary planning application for Ho Chi Minh City.
At the time of the meeting, the project was in its early development stage, with initial components such as the user interface and Backend structure taking shape.
The presentations provided useful concepts that I could consider during future development.
In particular, I realized the importance of separating system responsibilities, managing data carefully, and controlling how user requests are processed.
The security-related topics also encouraged me to pay more attention to system design and potential risks before deployment.
However, these technologies were primarily topics I explored during the meeting. They do not represent features or AWS services that I have already implemented in my project.
7. Personal Reflection What interested me most about the FCAJ Mini Meeting was how the speakers explained the practical challenges behind real-world AI applications.
Previously, when learning about AI, I mainly focused on the models themselves. However, the Voice AI and AI Agent presentations helped me understand that many other components are necessary for a complete system.
Some topics, such as AWS RAM and AgentCore Memory, were still new to me. I would need to study additional documentation to better understand their practical applications.
Overall, the meeting broadened my knowledge of AI and AWS and gave me additional direction for future learning and project development.

title: Access S3 from on-premises
content:
Overview In this section, you will create an Interface endpoint to access Amazon S3 from a simulated on-premises environment. The Interface endpoint will allow you to route to Amazon S3 over a VPN connection from your simulated on-premises environment.
Why using Interface endpoint:
Gateway endpoints only work with resources running in the VPC where they are created. Interface endpoints work with resources running in VPC, and also resources running in on-premises environments. Connectivty from your on-premises environment to the cloud can be provided by AWS Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Interface endpoints allow you to connect to services powered by AWS PrivateLink. These services include some AWS services, services hosted by other AWS customers and partners in their own VPCs (referred to as PrivateLink Endpoint Services), and supported AWS Marketplace Partner services. For this workshop, we will focus on connecting to Amazon S3.

title: On-premises DNS Simulation
content:
AWS PrivateLink endpoints have a fixed IP address in each Availability Zone where they are deployed, for the life of the endpoint (until it is deleted). These IP addresses are attached to Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs). AWS recommends using DNS to resolve the IP addresses for endpoints so that downstream applications use the latest IP addresses when ENIs are added to new AZs, or deleted over time.
In this section, you will create a forwarding rule to send DNS resolution requests from a simulated on-premises environment to a Route 53 Private Hosted Zone. This section leverages the infrastructure deployed by CloudFormation in the Prepare the environment section.
Create DNS Alias Records for the Interface endpoint Navigate to the Route 53 management console (Hosted Zones section). The CloudFormation template you deployed in the Prepare the environment section created this Private Hosted Zone. Click on the name of the Private Hosted Zone, s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com: Create a new record in the Private Hosted Zone: Record name and record type keep default options Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor (you saved when doing section 4.3) Click Add another record, and add a second record using the following values. Click Create records when finished to create both records. Record name: *. Record type: keep default value (type A) Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor The new records appear in the Route 53 console:
Create a Resolver Forwarding Rule Route 53 Resolver Forwarding Rules allow you to forward DNS queries from your VPC to other sources for name resolution. Outside of a workshop environment, you might use this feature to forward DNS queries from your VPC to DNS servers running on-premises. In this section, you will simulate an on-premises conditional forwarder by creating a forwarding rule that forwards DNS queries for Amazon S3 to a Private Hosted Zone running in “VPC Cloud” in-order to resolve the PrivateLink interface endpoint regional DNS name.
From the Route 53 management console, click Inbound endpoints on the left side bar In the Inbound endpoints console, click the ID of the inbound endpoint Copy the two IP addresses listed to your text editor From the Route 53 menu, choose Resolver > Rules, and click Create rule: In the Create rule console: Name: myS3Rule Rule type: Forward Domain name: s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com VPC: VPC On-prem Outbound endpoint: VPCOnpremOutboundEndpoint Target IP Addresses: Enter both IP addresses from your text editor (inbound endpoint addresses) and then click Submit You have successfully created resolver forwarding rule.
Test the on-premises DNS Simulation Connect to Test-Interface-Endpoint EC2 instance with Session manager Test DNS resolution. The dig command will return the IP addresses assigned to the VPC Interface endpoint running in VPC Cloud (your IP’s will be different): dig +short s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com The IP addresses returned are the VPC endpoint IP addresses, NOT the Resolver IP addresses you pasted from your text editor. The IP addresses of the Resolver endpoint and the VPC endpoint look similar because they are all from the VPC Cloud CIDR block.
Navigate to the VPC menu (Endpoints section), select the S3 Interface endpoint. Click the Subnets tab and verify that the IP addresses returned by Dig match the VPC endpoint: Return to your shell and use the AWS CLI to test listing your S3 buckets: aws s3 ls --endpoint-url https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com Terminate your Session Manager session: In this section you created an Interface endpoint for Amazon S3. This endpoint can be reached from on-premises through Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoints simulated forwarding DNS requests from on-premises to a Private Hosted Zone running the cloud. Route 53 inbound Endpoints recieved the resolution request and returned a response containing the IP addresses of the VPC interface endpoint. Using DNS to resolve the endpoint IP addresses provides high availability in-case of an Availability Zone outage.

title: VPC Endpoint Policies
content:
When you create an interface or gateway endpoint, you can attach an endpoint policy to it that controls access to the service to which you are connecting. A VPC endpoint policy is an IAM resource policy that you attach to an endpoint. If you do not attach a policy when you create an endpoint, AWS attaches a default policy for you that allows full access to the service through the endpoint.
You can create a policy that restricts access to specific S3 buckets only. This is useful if you only want certain S3 Buckets to be accessible through the endpoint.
In this section you will create a VPC endpoint policy that restricts access to the S3 bucket specified in the VPC endpoint policy.
Connect to an EC2 instance and verify connectivity to S3 Start a new AWS Session Manager session on the instance named Test-Gateway-Endpoint. From the session, verify that you can list the contents of the bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC: aws s3 ls s3://\<your-bucket-name\> The bucket contents include the two 1 GB files uploaded in earlier.
Create a new S3 bucket; follow the naming pattern you used in Part 1, but add a ‘-2’ to the name. Leave other fields as default and click create Successfully create bucket
Navigate to: Services > VPC > Endpoints, then select the Gateway VPC endpoint you created earlier. Click the Policy tab. Click Edit policy. The default policy allows access to all S3 Buckets through the VPC endpoint.
In Edit Policy console, copy & Paste the following policy, then replace yourbucketname-2 with your 2nd bucket name. This policy will allow access through the VPC endpoint to your new bucket, but not any other bucket in Amazon S3. Click Save to apply the policy. { "Id": "Policy1631305502445", "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "Stmt1631305501021", "Action": "s3:*", "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2", "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2/*" ], "Principal": "*" } ] } Successfully customize policy
From your session on the Test-Gateway-Endpoint instance, test access to the S3 bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC aws s3 ls s3://<yourbucketname> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy:
Return to your home directory on your EC2 instance cd~ Create a file fallocate -l 1G test-bucket2.xyz Copy file to 2nd bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-2nd-bucket-name> This operation succeeds because it is permitted by the VPC endpoint policy.
Then we test access to the first bucket by copy the file to 1st bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-1st-bucket-name> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy.
Part 3 Summary: In this section, you created a VPC endpoint policy for Amazon S3, and used the AWS CLI to test the policy. AWS CLI actions targeted to your original S3 bucket failed because you applied a policy that only allowed access to the second bucket you created. AWS CLI actions targeted for your second bucket succeeded because the policy allowed them. These policies can be useful in situations where you need to control access to resources through VPC endpoints.

Starting with a small JSON example and tracing how it enters the Handler made the process easier to follow. Reviewing the Lambda Proxy Integration example and breaking the flow into receiving the request, invoking the Function, and returning the result helped clarify each service’s responsibility.

title: Week 9 Worklog
content:
Week 9 Objectives: Learn how AWS services send and receive messages. Become familiar with Amazon SQS, SNS, and SES and their basic use cases. Understand how Amazon EventBridge helps services respond to events. Learn when to use each service and check costs before hands-on practice. Tasks to Be Completed This Week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference 2 Learn about Amazon SQS and how messages are stored in a Queue for later processing. Review an example of an online store’s order queue. 09/11/2026 09/11/2026 Amazon SQS 3 Learn about Standard Queues, FIFO Queues, and Visibility Timeout. Read an example explaining why a message should be deleted after processing. 10/11/2026 10/11/2026 SQS Visibility Timeout 4 Learn about Amazon SNS, Topics, and Subscriptions. Review an example of sending one notification to several people or services. 11/11/2026 11/11/2026 Amazon SNS 5 Learn about Amazon SES and how applications send confirmation or notification emails. Read about email verification and Sandbox limits without sending actual emails. 12/11/2026 12/11/2026 Amazon SES, SES Sandbox 6 Learn about Amazon EventBridge, Event Buses, Rules, and Targets. Review an example of an AWS event being sent to Lambda or SQS when it matches a rule. 13/11/2026 13/11/2026 Amazon EventBridge 7 Review and compare SQS, SNS, SES, and EventBridge using simple examples. Read about pricing and Free Tier limits without creating Queues, Topics, or Event Rules on AWS. 14/11/2026 14/11/2026 AWS Messaging Decision Guide, EventBridge Pricing Week 9 Achievements: Knowledge Gained:
Understood that SQS stores messages in a Queue so a consumer can process them when ready, without both parts of the system needing to run at the same time. Learned that Standard Queues suit many common tasks, while FIFO Queues help keep messages in order within a message group. Understood the basic purpose of Visibility Timeout. Learned that SNS uses Topics and Subscriptions to send one notification to several destinations, such as email or SQS. Understood that SES can send emails from an application, such as sign-up confirmation emails. Sandbox accounts have recipient restrictions and require appropriate address verification. Learned that EventBridge receives events and uses Rules to send them to suitable Targets, such as Lambda or SQS. Review and Learning with the Materials:
Reviewed an online ordering example where SQS holds orders until a consumer is ready to process them. Compared how SNS sends notifications with how EventBridge routes events based on rules. Checked pricing and free usage limits. This week focused on reading documentation, without creating AWS resources or sending emails to avoid unexpected costs. Challenges Encountered and Solutions:
Visibility Timeout took extra reading because a message stays in the Queue even after it has been received. An example showing that messages are deleted after processing helped me understand why. SNS and EventBridge can both send information to other services, so choosing between them was not immediately clear. The examples showed me that SNS is useful for Topic-based notifications, while EventBridge helps filter and route events using Rules.
